"Even with zero Primary One classes, we must become a deluxe version of an estate school"

Ahead of the merger, SKH Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School is adopting "counter-cyclical" measures. Principal Kwong Ka-man said the new school year will see an investment of HK$1.8 million to enrich students' diverse learning experiences: the school football pitch will be opened for students to ride bicycles, free enhanced athletics training will be provided, the entire school will be subsidised to learn swimming, and the English-language curriculum will be strengthened.

The principal said: "Even with zero Primary One classes, we must build the most wonderful school — a deluxe version of an estate school." The HK$1.8 million mainly comes from Education Bureau grants, school reserves and donations.

On the first day of school, students who had just moved up a year felt mixed emotions. Student Wu, knowing the school is under-enrolled and about to close, said she felt "both happy and sad". "I'm happy because in the future there might be more classmates and it could be livelier; I'm sad because I can't bear to see such a big school just disappear like this."

The unforgettable 'Kei Tak' classroom

Recalling her days at Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School, student Wu said what she will remember most is the exchange tour to Xi'an that she went on with her teachers and classmates. Student Huang described how teachers would "teach through play", using games to help students learn. She hopes the Wong Tai Sin campus will have teachers as good as those at Kei Tak, and said what she will miss most is the "Kei Tak" classroom — "because of the friends there". Student Tse said: "Having studied at Kei Tak for several years, and then it's suddenly gone — I feel a bit sad."

Resources can be concentrated on existing students

Parents' feelings are equally complex. Ms Au, whose child is in Primary Six, said she was "heartbroken" upon hearing the news of zero classes, and felt shocked. She said: "The principal has just taken up her post, the school has been working so hard, yet this year 15 primary schools face the axe." She said the relationship between the parent body and the teaching team has been carefully built over the years, and everyone quickly adjusted. "In fact, you gain some things and you lose some things," and "since this is God's arrangement", she instead sees her child becoming more positive in adversity, and the school being able to focus resources on existing students rather than being tied down by enrolment issues.

"Why does it have to merge just because it can't recruit enough students?"

Mrs Wu has a child in Primary Four and an older son who has already graduated. She said her child felt the school had "a lot more care and attention" after returning to campus, and really likes the teachers and the principal. "At first, when we received the (school closure) news, I really felt a bit lost," she said. "Such a good school — why does it have to merge just because it can't recruit enough students?" What she appreciates most about Kei Tak is that it gives children confidence — "this kind of child is really lacking nowadays" — and her child isn't afraid of everything.

Concern about cross-district schooling in the future

Mrs Huang has children in Primary Four and Primary Six. She admitted being upset at first, feeling it was "really unfair". Mrs Huang said: "The school is so good, the children are so happy here, why don't other people know about it?" After adjusting her mindset, she believes "in crisis there is opportunity". The merger "may not be the best outcome", but since March this year, she has seen the school invite the entire school community to walk this path together, and the children have learned to face difficulties and challenges as one. She is grateful that Kei Tak has such close home-school ties, and that "we are not fighting alone".

Mrs Chung, who lives near the school, is more concerned about cross-district schooling in the future. She said the ideal would of course be to stay at Kei Tak — "we all live quite close by" — as it only takes five to ten minutes to walk to school. After the merger plan was announced, she took a bus to Wong Tai Sin to have a look and felt she "could accept it", with a bus ride of about 20 minutes followed by a short walk.

Strong sense of belonging to 'Kei Tak'

She had asked her daughter whether she wanted to transfer to another primary school in the same district. Her daughter said: "I don't want to leave this school," showing a strong sense of belonging to "Kei Tak". Mrs Chung respects her daughter's choice and will accompany her through it. The school has mentioned possible school bus and uniform subsidies, but the details have yet to be finalised. Mrs Chung said that after crossing districts to Wong Tai Sin, the secondary school catchment net when choosing a secondary school may be wider — "treat it as an opportunity for her to step beyond this district". She also mentioned that class sizes are currently very small, and after moving to Wong Tai Sin the classes may be larger and her daughter will have to readjust. But she believes her daughter has already learned to be independent at Kei Tak, so she is "not that worried".

Principal: Focus on doing well in the future

Principal Kwong Ka-man, herself a former student, admitted that zero classes "is not good news for a school", but stressed that the key is how to turn things around: "We are focused on doing well in the future." She does not want to tell a tragic story — "in reality, we are all very positive" — and noted that the news did not come out of nowhere; teachers and students have had time to digest it.

After the Primary Six graduates leave, the school will have 121 students for the basic school year, with six transfer students enrolled: one in Primary Two, four in Primary Five and one in Primary Six. Kwong Ka-man said the overall attrition rate for Primary Two to Six is similar to previous years, with about ten students leaving during the summer, of whom two were moving house and the rest transferred to other districts.

Formerly the Wong Tai Sin Kei Tak AM school

Asked whether it was the merger news that "scared students away", she said one cannot generalise. She pointed out that the secondary school catchment in Sai Kung district has never been as attractive as that in Kwun Tong or "across the harbour". "When the whole territory doesn't have enough students, it's like musical chairs going round and round." Some parents, even as they departed, still said they had confidence in the school; they simply wanted their children to study in another district.

"Kei Tak" was formerly the Wong Tai Sin Kei Tak AM school. In 2004, the government allocated the Tseung Kwan O school premises, and the two schools split to become whole-day schools. Kwong Ka-man said the Wong Tai Sin school "is actually our alma mater", sharing the same sponsoring body and the same roots, which makes the merger relatively easy to handle. Over the next three years, the two schools will gradually increase joint student activities, collaborative lesson preparation and teaching research, so that students who need to move over in three years' time can adapt more easily.

Graduates allocated to Wong Tai Sin school net

The Education Bureau provides up to HK$1 million in support for each merger case, with details such as school bus subsidies still being finalised. She acknowledged that some parents find the distance too far and want to stay in Tseung Kwan O; but looking at it another way, after graduation students will be allocated places under the Wong Tai Sin school net, which may give them access to options in Kowloon City and beyond. Parents are mostly "watching cautiously" for now.

Among the 15 schools with zero Primary One classes, eight will be merged, including SKH Tseung Kwan O Kei Tak Primary School and SKH Kei Tak Primary School in Wong Tai Sin, which will merge across districts in a process expected to be completed in the 2029–2030 school year. In addition, four will be closed, two will run their own private Primary One classes, and one will continue to participate in Primary One allocation.
